The `Error` constructor already records the stack when `super()` runs. Calling `Error.captureStackTrace(this, MyError)` in the subclass's constructor does that work a second time.

The rule checks classes that extend a built-in error such as `Error`, `TypeError` or `RangeError`. It reports the call when the second argument is the class itself, written as its name, `new.target` or `this.constructor`.

`--fix-suggestions` removes the call.

{/* Generated by src/codegen/lint-rule-docs.ts. Do not edit this section. */}

## Configure

Off by default. To turn it on:

```toml bunfig.toml
[lint.rules]
"unicorn/no-useless-error-capture-stack-trace" = "error" # or "warn"
```

{/* End of the generated section. */}

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad */}
```js
class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(message) {
    super(message);
    this.name = "ValidationError";
    Error.captureStackTrace(this, ValidationError);
  }
}
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```js
class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(message) {
    super(message);
    this.name = "ValidationError";
  }
}
```

Hiding another function from the stack is a real use, and so is calling it in a class that doesn't extend a built-in error:

{/* good */}
```js
class ParseError extends SyntaxError {
  constructor(message) {
    super(message);
    Error.captureStackTrace(this, parse);
  }
}

class Failure {
  constructor() {
    Error.captureStackTrace(this, Failure);
  }
}
```
